It is argued that although these cities are separate political entities, they are economically and socially single communities and that traffic moving between them is intracommunity in nature and should be exempt from economic regulation. In support of this argument, these interests point out the extent to which these neighboring cities share utility companies, public transportation systems, and social and cultural activities.
The Nalco Chemical Company, a shipper of commodities in bulk, has plants located just outside the commercial zones of several large cities. It supports zone expansion because it will eliminate costly interline arrangements and also enable more shippers to take advantage of the generally lower rates which prevail on local movements within a zone. Expansion will also eliminate the competitive advantage enjoyed by shippers within the present zones over those shippers located just outside the zones. It also argues that expansion will result in an increase in bulk carrier service available to industries within the zones.
We stated in our Interim Report that it is not our intention to exclude from a commercial zone described under the proposed formula areas which we have previously determined to be commercially a part of a particular municipality. We redescribed the zones of nine cities along readily identifiable lines, in order to assure that no unintended contraction of commercial zone limits will occur by application of the proposed formula.
